details.label: Discussion
details.text: A long-lived supercell that has a history of producing large to very large hail across southwest SD is tracking southeastward, and should move into parts of the NE Panhandle/western NE in the next hour or so. Other convection is also ongoing along and perhaps just east of a weak surface boundary draped across western NE. Latest mesoanalysis estimates some lingering MLCIN across this region, which is evidenced by updrafts struggling to be sustained with southward extent in western NE. Still, some risk for large hail may continue with the well-established supercell moving southeastward out of southwest SD, as deep-layer shear remains strong. Trends are being monitored for possible watch issuance, with overall coverage of severe convection remaining uncertain

mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: Intense supercells will remain capable of producing mainly large to very large hail (up to 2-3.5 inches and diameter) this evening as they track east-southeastward

details.label: Summary
details.text: Intense supercells will remain capable of producing mainly large to very large hail (up to 2-3.5 inches and diameter) this evening as they track east-southeastward

details.label: Discussion
details.text: A supercell which developed over the Black Hills earlier this afternoon strengthened and produced large hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter in southwest SD. Since then, additional supercells have developed over far southeast MT into northwest SD, and over the Black Hills. The environment across western SD remains quite favorable for the maintenance for intense supercells this evening, with strong instability and deep-layer shear both present. These supercells are expected to generally track east-southeastward while posing a threat for mainly large to very large hail up to 2.5-3.5 inches in diameter. Some risk for severe/damaging winds will also exist with RFD surges with these intense cells

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Latest surface observations and radar/visible imagery depict an outflow boundary rapidly expanding westward as the cold pool associated with a robust MCS continues to expand. Across southwest IN, an organized, but compact MCS, southwest of Indianapolis has shown steadily declining velocities behind a bowing segment, suggesting that the complex is gradually weakening as it migrates further east into the cold pool. Additionally, new convection continues to develop along and behind the outflow boundary across northern KY. In general, this activity has exhibited transient intensification as buoyant parcels originating within the warm sector are quickly displaced into the cold pool. This trend should generally continue over the next couple of hours with most model solutions hinting at additional thunderstorm development through roughly 00-02 UTC. Storm motions into the cool/stable air mass should continue to limit storm longevity, but strong deep-layer wind shear across may support periodic storm organization with an attendant threat for large hail (most likely around 1 inch) and severe/damaging gusts. Although new watch issuance will likely not be needed, local expansions may be required as new convection emerges
